passage:
"Vidya, that's the fifth time you've looked at your phone since we sat down."

"Just checking. It dropped again. Look."

"You said you'd stop at lunch."

"I know. It's down a little and if I put a bit more in now I'll get it back when it climbs."

"Hm. And how was your mood this morning when it was green?"

"Fine. Great, actually."

"And now?"

Vidya stared at the red number. "Awful. My tea's gone cold and I haven't heard one word you said."

"That sounds less like planning and more like a slot machine, no?"

She was silent. Then she pressed and held the app icon. "Okay, Raghav. Notifications off, and I only look once at night. No more money in to fix it."

qa.q: How many times had Vidya looked at her phone since they sat down?
qa.a: Vidya had looked at her phone five times since they sat down.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when she said "Awful"?
qa.a: Vidya felt low because the red number had taken over her mood, so she stopped hearing Raghav and let her tea go cold.

qa.q: What limits does Vidya set, and why do they help?
qa.a: She turns off notifications, looks only once at night and adds no more money to fix a loss, which breaks the loop of checking and doubling down.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel watching Vidya check the app?
qa.a: Raghav probably feels worried and a little ignored, but keeps the questions gentle so Vidya can notice the pattern herself.

grounding: Vidya checks a trading app constantly and her mood follows the chart until she sees it as a gambling loop and sets limits.

passage: In the open-plan office of an insurance firm in Pune, Swati's phone lay face up beside her keyboard, the trading app's green and red lines glowing. She had checked it forty-one times before lunch. When the line dipped, her chest went tight and she snapped at a client on the phone; when it rose, she felt giddy enough to buy samosas for the whole row. Her team lead, Jaya, noticed. At the tea machine, Jaya said, 'Your mood's been riding that chart all week.' Swati laughed, then didn't. 'I lost some yesterday. I was going to put in double today to win it back.' Jaya was quiet a moment. 'That sounds more like a slot machine than a plan.' Swati felt her face heat. Back at her desk, she turned off the app's notifications, moved it off her home screen, and allowed herself two checks a day, after lunch and after work. She didn't put in double.

qa.q: How many times had Swati checked the app before lunch?
qa.a: Swati had checked it forty-one times before lunch.

qa.q: What did Swati feel when the line dipped?
qa.a: Swati felt tense and irritable, her chest going tight, enough to snap at a client.

qa.q: What limits did Swati set, and why are they wise?
qa.a: She turned off notifications, moved the app off her home screen and allowed two checks a day, which breaks the gambling-like loop.

qa.q: How does Jaya see Swati's behaviour?
qa.a: Jaya sees Swati's mood riding the chart and worries it is more like a slot machine than a plan.

grounding: Shows constant checking of a trading app with mood following the chart, and Swati noticing the gambling-like loop and setting limits instead of doubling down.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal,
Remember you asked why I stopped answering during movie nights? Here's the honest reason.
Since March I've been trading on my phone. At first it was fun. Then I noticed I was checking the app every few minutes, in class, in the bathroom, at 3 a.m. When it went up, I felt brilliant. When it went down, I couldn't eat. Last week I lost a chunk, and my first thought was to put in twice as much to win it back. That scared me, because it's exactly how my uncle talks about card games.
So I've done three things. Notifications off. The app is deleted from my phone; I can only check on my laptop, once a day, after dinner. And I've asked my cousin, who works at a bank, to ask me every Sunday how it's going.
I'm not sure I'm done with it. But I don't want my mood run by a chart.
Come for movie night on Friday?
Tenzin

qa.q: When does Tenzin now check the app?
qa.a: Tenzin now checks only on the laptop, once a day, after dinner.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling after wanting to put in twice as much?
qa.a: Tenzin felt scared, recognising the same pattern an uncle shows with card games.

qa.q: Which of Tenzin's three steps seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Turning off notifications and deleting the app from the phone, because it breaks the constant checking loop.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Ujjwal might feel relieved to know why Tenzin went quiet, and glad to be invited back to movie night.

grounding: A letter shows obsessive checking of a trading app, the urge to double down after a loss, and Tenzin setting limits and asking for support.
